---
title: "Gendered language in performance feedback"
subtitle: "Research collaboration with Culture Amp"
description: "Applying NLP to large-scale performance feedback to show how manager and employee gender shape the language of workplace evaluations."
categories: [NLP, People analytics, Python, Mixed-effects models]

## Overview

Performance feedback shapes pay, promotion and development, yet research on
gender bias in feedback mostly relies on small, manually coded samples. I set
up a research collaboration with Culture Amp to study this question at scale,
using natural language processing (NLP) on written feedback from organisations
that use its platform. The work forms the core of my PhD at the University of
Melbourne.

## The question

Do managers write about women and men differently, and does the manager's own
gender matter? I examine the content, tone and linguistic style of feedback,
and the organisational factors, such as team size, that may explain gender
differences.

## Approach

- **Text processing pipeline:** cleaning, anonymisation and linguistic
  annotation of feedback texts (spaCy, LLM-based name extraction).
- **Content:** agentic and communal language measured with sentence embeddings,
  distinctive vocabulary with weighted log-odds, and themes with topic
  modelling (NMF, BERTopic).
- **Tone:** sentiment and emotion classified with transformer models
  (RoBERTa, GoEmotions), and valence and arousal scored with lexicons.
- **Style:** hedging, elaboration, lexical diversity and grammatical
  complexity.
- **Inference:** mixed-effects and GEE models that account for the clustering
  of feedback within manager–employee pairs, and mediation analysis for
  organisational mechanisms.

## Key findings

- **Manager gender often predicts feedback language more strongly than
  employee gender.** Who writes the feedback matters as much as who receives
  it.
- **Female managers write longer, more positive feedback and hedge more**, and
  hedging is strongest when female managers write about female employees.
- **Team size helps explain gender differences.** Male managers oversee larger
  teams, and span of control partly accounts for differences in how managers
  frame their feedback.

## Why it matters

These findings suggest that efforts to reduce bias in performance reviews
should look at the people who write feedback, not only at those who receive
it. They also show how NLP can turn unstructured feedback into evidence that
organisations can act on, for example in reviewer guidance, calibration
sessions and DEI reporting.

## My role

I designed the research collaboration, built the full analysis pipeline in
Python, and led all analyses and write-up, working with supervisors at the
University of Melbourne and UC Berkeley Haas.
